title: Momoni
author: Ghanaian tradition
desc: Fresh fish salted at about 22.5 per cent and fermented seven days at thirty-five degrees — the good endpoint smells of processing odour and sour milk, not sulphur.
longDesc: Momoni is the fermented salted fish that gives Ghanaian stews their deepest savoury note, and it is published here as a documented process. The best endpoint comes from a 2024 study which found that the optimal sensory results used fresh fish, twenty-two and a half per cent salt and seven days of fermentation at thirty-five degrees — the same conditions as currently practised in Ghana. The cue is an odour: good momoni carries a processing odour with mild trimethylamine and a note of sour milk; bad momoni smells of high trimethylamine and rotten sulphur. The pH figures across five studies do not agree at all.
ingredients: Fresh fish — kingfish or jack mackerel are documented, gutted and cut into pieces
Salt, at about 22.5 per cent of the fish weight
// Further salt at about three quarters of the initial weight, for the resalting route
// No household quantities are published. See the note.
steps: Gut and wash the fish and cut it into pieces.
Leave overnight at room temperature in a fly-free enclosure.
Salt at about 22.5 per cent of the fish weight.
Place in a plastic bucket and leave undisturbed three days.
// Alternative documented route: on the third day remove and wash the fish, then resalt at about three quarters of the initial salt weight and ferment a further ten days.
Ferment about seven days total at around 35 degrees for the optimised process.
// ENDPOINT, by smell: good momoni has a processing odour with mild trimethylamine and a note of sour milk. Reject it if it smells of high trimethylamine or rotten sulphur.
Dry if a dried product is wanted.
Use in small quantities as a savoury seasoning.
chefTips: The endpoint is a smell and the distinction is specific: good momoni gives a processing odour with mild trimethylamine and a sour-milk note. Rotten sulphur or a strong fishy ammonia means it has gone wrong.
Fresh fish, not fish that has sat about. The 2024 study compared fresh fish against fish stored twenty-four hours unpreserved and found fresh gave the better result.
Twenty-two and a half per cent salt by fish weight is the optimised figure, and the study notes this matches what is already practised in Ghana.
Seven days at thirty-five degrees. That is the optimised combination; the older documented route is three days salted, then washing, resalting and ten more days.
A fly-free enclosure for the overnight stage. This is an open fermentation and insects are the main spoilage risk.
The pH literature does not agree — above 7, above 6, falling from 6.5 to 5.2, and 7.1 to 7.8 across four studies. Do not use pH as your test; use the smell.
Use it sparingly. A piece the size of a thumb seasons a whole pot, and more makes a stew inedible.
commonMistakes: Using fish that is no longer fresh.
Under-salting, which lets spoilage organisms win.
Fermenting uncovered where flies can reach it.
Trusting a pH figure, given how widely the published values differ.
Using too much in a dish.
sources: PUBLISHED AS A DOCUMENTED PROCESS, NOT A HOUSEHOLD RECIPE. No named source publishes home quantities; none have been invented, and the ingredient list says so.

THE ENDPOINT CUE, which is what makes this fermentation publishable: Arthur, Edna, with Margrét Geirsdóttir on the accompanying poster, 'Assessment of the fermentation value chain in micro to small-scale fish processing facilities in Ghana, and its impact on product quality', GRÓ FTP, 2024. ABSTRACT TWO-PASS; the POSTER DETAILS ARE SINGLE-PASS AND UNVERIFIED, which matters because the temperature and the cue wording come from the poster.

Abstract figures, TWO-PASS: salt at '17.5%, 22.5%, and 27.5%'; 'fermentation durations of 3, 6, and 7 days'; fresh fish compared against fish 'stored for 24 hours without preservation'; 'pH varied significantly (p=0.00)'.

Poster, SINGLE-PASS, verbatim: temperature 35°C, and 'Optimal sensory results were obtained for samples using fresh fish, 22,5% salt and 7 days of fermentation, the same conditions as currently practiced in Ghana.' GOOD ATTRIBUTES: 'processing odour with mild TMA, and sour milk'. BAD: 'high TMA, rotten sulphur odour'. The abstract's second pass also lists 'unpleasant odours (TMA, sulphur)' and 'sour milk'. The poster states NO pH values. TMA is trimethylamine, the compound responsible for the smell of spoiling fish.

THE OLDER DOCUMENTED ROUTE: Abbey L.D., Hodari-Okae M.A., Osei-Yaw A., 'Studies on Traditional Processing and Quality of Fermented Fish', Food Research Institute, CSIR, Accra, December 1994. TWO-PASS. Process verbatim: 'Fish were gutted, washed and cut into 3 pieces. These were left overnight at room temperature in a fly free enclosure.' 'The salted fish were placed in a plastic bucket ... left undisturbed for three days.' 'On the third day, the fish were removed and washed. This was followed by resalting but in this case the salt quantities were reduced to about three-quarters of the initial weights.' '... allowed to ferment for a further 10 days.' SALT: three ratios tested at 15%, 25% and 40%; 'A 25% salt to fish weight and over was considered appropriate for the production of momone.' pH: 'above pH of 7'. TVB-N 277.5-438.2 mg/kg (one pass only). Species, one pass only: kingfish (Scomberomorus tritor) and jack mackerel (Caranx hippos).

ITS SENSORY TIME COURSE, as printed: day 1 'Shiny colour Rotten smell Slimy'; day 5 'Brownnish Less pungent Watery'; 'Soft texture' throughout. NOTE that this is a time course of observations rather than an explicit endpoint, and the two fetches framed it differently.

THE pH LITERATURE DOES NOT AGREE, and this is why the tips say not to rely on it. (1) Abbey 1994: 'above pH of 7'. (2) Sanni A.I., Asiedu M., Ayernor G.S., 'Microflora and chemical composition of Momoni, a Ghanaian fermented fish condiment', Journal of Food Composition and Analysis, October 2002, TWO-PASS, retail samples: 'moisture content of 50%, protein values of 16.8-21.9%, a titratable acidity of 2%, and a pH of above 6.0', with a 'high salt content of momoni (294-310 g/kg)' and lactic acid bacteria at 10^3 cfu/g. They conclude the fermentation 'is mediated by the endogenous enzymes of the fish rather than the associated micro-organisms' — which is a significant finding: momoni is largely an enzymatic rather than a microbial fermentation. (3) Asiedu B.K. and ten co-authors, 'Momoni as a model for African fermented fish: Nutritional composition, bioactive metabolites and safety perspectives', Journal of Food Composition and Analysis 149:108612, January 2026, abstract TWO-PASS: 'pH fall from 6.5 to 5.2', free amino acids 'from 18 to 45 mg/g', 'high salt content (10–20 %)'. (4) Nerquaye-Tetteh G., Eyeson K.K., Tete-Marmon J., Ghana Journal of Agricultural Science 11:21-26, 1978, TWO-PASS on ranges: salt 'ranged from 2 kg to 8 kg per 18 kg of fresh fish'; 'The duration of fermentation varied from 6 h to 8 days'; drying 'from 3 to 10 days'. Its pH of '7.1-7.8' is SINGLE-PASS; the other fetch said only 'similar to those reported for spoiled temperate marine fish'. FLAG: that paper's title prints as 'Bornone' and its abstract text is OCR-garbled ('Homonc production'), so the product identification is UNVERIFIED though presumably momone.

THE FULL UNRECONCILED SPREAD. SALT: 15/25/40% with ≥25% judged appropriate (Abbey); 17.5/22.5/27.5% with 22.5% optimal (Arthur); 294-310 g/kg in retail product (Sanni); '10-20%' (Asiedu 2026); 2-8 kg per 18 kg fish (Nerquaye-Tetteh). TIME: 3 days plus 10 with resalting (Abbey); 7 days at 35°C (Arthur); 6 hours to 8 days as surveyed (Nerquaye-Tetteh). pH: above 7, above 6.0, falling 6.5 to 5.2, and 7.1-7.8. NOTHING IS AVERAGED and the smell cue is offered as the practical test precisely because the measured figures conflict.

A RELATED PRODUCT NOT PUBLISHED: koobi and kako, salted dried tilapia and other fish, were REFUSED. The only koobi-adjacent paper reached (Nerquaye-Tetteh, Ghana Journal of Agricultural Science 11) gives 'Salting takes 1-7 days' and 'Drying 3-8 days' with NO pH figure and NO endpoint cue, so there is nothing publishable.
storage: Months, given the salt content. Keep sealed and cool.
reheating: Not applicable. Used as a seasoning.
healthBenefits: Very high in protein at 16.8 to 21.9 per cent in retail samples.
Fermentation raises free amino acids substantially, from 18 to 45 mg/g in one study.
A source of iodine and omega-3 fats.
Used in tiny quantities, so the very high salt contributes little per serving.
culturalNote: Momoni is the ingredient that makes a Ghanaian stew taste Ghanaian, and it is also the one that empties a kitchen when the jar is opened. That one study concludes the fermentation is driven by the fish's own enzymes rather than by microbes is a genuinely interesting finding — it means momoni is closer to a fish sauce than to a yoghurt.
